tree.name: MenuBar
tree.doc:
The record-driven menu bar: **whole menus are data** —

    menus = { [ ({ id, label, bold?, items: [ …menu records… ] }), … ] }

— and the component arranges. One internal Menu serves every title; its
`items` constraint derives from the open title's record, so item state
(enabled, checked, labels) stays live while the menu is up. Because the
records are the single declaration, an app can derive its key registry
from the same array the bar renders — nothing is declared twice.

Tracking is the classic desktop behavior: titles do not highlight on mere hover;
a click opens (and highlights) a title; while any menu is open, moving
across another title switches to it; clicking the open title closes.

Delivery is the one seam: `picked(id)` — override at the use site.

A dropped menu paints over the bar's later siblings: the bar raises itself when a menu
opens (stacking is source order, and `raise()` is the runtime verb for it). A bar nested
inside a container that sits under other content wants that container declared last,
or a menu hosted at the app layer as `Combobox` does.

```declare
App [ width = 380, height = 190, chose: string = "",
    bar: MenuBar [ x = 12, y = 8,
        menus = { [ ({ id: "file", label: "File", items: [ ({ id: "new", label: "New", key: "⌘N" }),
                                                          ({ id: "open", label: "Open…" }) ] }),
                    ({ id: "edit", label: "Edit", items: [ ({ id: "undo", label: "Undo" }),
                                                           ({ divider: true }),
                                                           ({ id: "cut", label: "Cut" }) ] }) ] },
        picked(id: string) { app.chose = id }
        ],
    Text [ x = 20, y = 70, text = { app.chose == "" ? "nothing picked" : "picked: " + app.chose } ]
    ]
```

tree.name: Dialog
tree.doc:
The modal tier: a full-app scrim that swallows every press — modal input
blocking, no light dismiss — under a centered panel with a focus trap.
Buttons are **records** (the records door): `{ id, label, default?, cancel? }`,
rendered as themed library Buttons right-aligned in the platform arrangement.
Focus is saved on open and restored on close.

Keyboard: Return picks the default button (the Cupertino rule; a focused
button also activates on Space/Enter — the pick guard makes the double
harmless), Escape picks the cancel record when one exists, else just
closes.

The idioms — one verb each, an optional callback receiving the picked id
(the `picked(id)` override remains the declarative seam):

    dlg.notice("Saved", "Your changes were saved.")
    dlg.ask("Save changes?", "Unsaved changes will be lost.", (id) => …)
    dlg.error("Could not connect", "The server refused the connection.")

`ask` is Cancel / No / Yes-default; `error` renders the title in the
theme's errorColor.

**Platform structure is data**: `dialogWidth`, `dialogButtons` = `"end"` (a
right-aligned row — San Francisco, Material) | `"stack"` (the stacked alert —
full-width buttons stacked, default on top) | `"fill"` (WinUI ContentDialog —
equal-width buttons filling the row), `dialogAlign` = `"left"` | `"center"`
(the Cupertino centered title), `dialogTitleSize` / `dialogBodySize`. Plus
`scrimColor` + `scrimOpacity` (Cupertino barely dims — alerts separate by
shadow; Material's scrim is 32%; Fluent's smoke 30%), the `menuShadow` family,
`errorColor`.

**Declare one and call it.** A `Dialog` is not a view you show and hide around your
content — it is a standing member you open with a verb, so the same instance serves
every prompt in the program.

```declare
App [ width = 520, height = 260, said: string = "",
    dlg: Dialog [ ],
    Button [ x = 20, y = 20, label = "Delete…",
        onClick() { app.dlg.ask("Delete this file?", "This cannot be undone.",
                                (id) => { app.said = id }) }
        ],
    Text [ x = 20, y = 80, text = { app.said == "" ? "—" : "you chose: " + app.said } ]
    ]
```

tree.name: AppIsland
tree.doc:
`AppIsland` embeds a live Declare application: give it a `program` and it mounts
that program as its own child app — its own reactive graph, input router, and
stage — sized to this view's box. There is no coordinate sync: the tenant fills
the box, so your width/height constraints size it like any view.

It composes `DOMIsland` (the sanctioned foreign-content leaf) and builds the
host's mount key from structured inputs, so callers never hand-splice the
`run:…` wire. The page host (`browser/host-client.js`) sees the key on the box,
resolves the program on its boot ladder — prewarm → cache → in-browser compile,
identical on the dev server and a static host — and renders the child.

`childName` (inherited from `DOMIsland`) is the reverse channel: the running child's
`appName` reflected back up, so a host can title itself by what it shows.

### The bridge

An AppIsland carries the **island bridge** (guide ch. 18): declare `external`
attributes on the instance and they pair, by name and with a type handshake,
against the tenant program's own `external` declarations — typed facts both
ways, per settle. `post(topic, payload)` / `onPost(m: IslandPost)` carry the
verbs. `env` and `childName` below are untyped channels beside the bridge;
declare `external` attributes wherever the type matters.

The window frame, activation, and titling belong to the caller — a desktop window
adds an `onPointerDown` that raises itself and reads `childName` for its title; the
homepage and the viewer just size the box. This primitive is only the embedding.

attributes.name: program
attributes.doc:

real app — **no copy of the source, ever**), or the reserved `"__raw__"` live-edit

view of itself.

tree.name: SimpleLayout
tree.doc:
The stacking idiom: siblings placed one after another along
`axis`, in child order, `spacing` apart (negative overlaps). The cross axis
and all sizes stay the children's own — a child centers itself across a row
with the ordinary `y = center`. Invisible children are skipped and their
space reclaimed; a skipped child still gets the slot it would occupy, so
re-showing it needs no special case. A `Spacer` child flexes to absorb the
run's slack along the axis (between two groups it pushes them apart; one on
each side centers the run).

Written in Declare over the Layout kernel: the whole strategy is this one
pure place() — one box per laid child, aligned by index.

```declare
col: View [ x = 20, y = 20,
    layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 8 ],
    View [ width = 160, height = 24, cornerRadius = 6, fill = steelblue ],
    View [ width = 120, height = 24, cornerRadius = 6, fill = cadetblue ],
    View [ width = 190, height = 24, cornerRadius = 6, fill = slategray ]
    ]
```

attributes.name: axis
attributes.doc:
Which way children stack: `y` (the default) or `x`. **A bare literal, not a string** —
`axis = x`, and note that `x` here is the axis token, not the position attribute.

docSegs.md:

`axis = x`, and note that `x` here is the axis token, not the position attribute.

attributes.name: spacing
attributes.doc:
The gap between adjacent children. **Negative overlaps them**, which is how a stack of
cards or avatars is built.

docSegs.md:
The gap between adjacent children. **Negative overlaps them**, which is how a stack of
cards or avatars is built.

attributes.name: align
attributes.doc:
The **cross axis** — `y` on a row, `x` on a stack. `none` (the default) leaves it to the
children, who place themselves with the ordinary `y = center`. `start | center | end`
aligns every child within the **band**: the view's own cross extent — so a column
`width = 260` centres a `width = { parent.width - 32 }` child at 16, with the inset split
evenly — falling back to the **line**, the tallest (widest) laid child's extent, on a view
that derives its own cross size from these very children (reading an extent this
arrangement feeds would be a cycle, and on such a view the line *is* that extent). A
child wider than the band keeps the line, so it never hangs out both sides.
`baseline` — a row only — sits every child on one
baseline: a `Text` reports its own, and a composite **declares** which part carries it
(`baseline: number = { cap.y + cap.baseline }`); a laid child that declares none is
refused by name, at the child, and the checker says so before anything runs. A bare
literal.

methods.name: place
methods.doc:
The whole strategy: one box per laid child, positioned along the axis in child order.
**Every size stays the children's own, and so does the cross axis unless `align` says
otherwise** — then the boxes carry that slot too, and own it. Override it in a subclass
for custom geometry; a `Layout`'s `place()` **may** aggregate over children, which is the
one place that is allowed.

        layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 10 ],

        Bar [ width = 320, label = "east",  value = 50, tint = dodgerblue ],

tree.name: WrappingLayout
tree.doc:
A horizontal flow that **wraps**: children run left to right `spacing` apart,
and when the next one would overflow the view's width it drops to a new row
(`lineSpacing` down; -1, the default, means "same as spacing"). With room for
one row it is a plain row; as the view narrows it stacks — cards that reflow
on a phone with no media query. It owns both axes of each child (a flow is
2-D); sizes stay the children's own. `justify`
sets each finished row along the flow — `start`, `center`, `end`, or `fill`,
which spreads a row's slack into its gaps the way justified text does;
`indent` and `hangingIndent` inset the first row and every row after it, the
two shapes a paragraph takes.

Division of labor: this is the tool for uniform, replicated collections
that reflow by fitting. Managing named regions per width tier is
ResponsiveLayout's.

Written in Declare over the Layout kernel — the whole strategy is place().

```declare
box: View [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 260,
    layout: WrappingLayout [ spacing = 8, lineSpacing = 8 ],
    View [ width = 70, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = steelblue ],
    View [ width = 110, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = cadetblue ],
    View [ width = 90, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = slategray ],
    View [ width = 120, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = darkslateblue ]
    ]
```

uniform grid needs one number rather than two kept in step.

attributes.name: justify
attributes.doc:
How a finished row sits along the flow: `start` (the default, left), `center`, `end`
(right), or `fill` — the row's slack is spread evenly into the gaps between its
children, so every full row ends flush at the right edge, as justified text does. As
in text, the last row is left at `start` under `fill` (a ragged last line), and a row
of one child has no gap to widen and stays put. A bare literal.

attributes.doc:
Where each child sits **within its row**: `start` (the default — the row's top),
`center`, `end`, or `baseline`, which sits every child in the row on one baseline — a
`Text` reports its own, a composite **declares** which part carries it
(`baseline: number = { cap.y + cap.baseline }`), and a child that declares none is
refused by name and placed at the row's top. A row's height grows to hold the
baseline-shifted children. When the flow **never wrapped** — one row, which is the whole
content — `center` and `end` align it in the view's own height instead, so a single row
in a `height = 90` bar really sits in the middle of it; a view that derives its height
from this flow keeps the row as the band. A bare literal.

methods.name: place
methods.doc:
Runs the flow, wrapping when the next child would overflow the view's width. **It owns
both axes of each child** — a flow is 2-D — while sizes stay the children's own. A child
never wraps when it is first in its row, so one over-wide child overflows rather than
looping forever. Each finished row starts at its indent, is justified along the flow, and
has its children aligned across it, in one pass over the row.

tree.name: ResponsiveLayout
tree.doc:
A view's children often want one arrangement when there is room and another
when there isn't: three panels side by side on a wide screen, the same panels
stacked on a phone; an optional control that appears only when space allows.
ResponsiveLayout states those alternatives directly. You give it a list of
**plans** — each one says *"from this width up, arrange the children like
this"* — and it keeps the right plan applied as the view's width changes.
Hiding, showing, and dividing the width are all part of a plan, not separate
wiring.

    bar: View [
        layout: ResponsiveLayout [ plan = { [
            { from: 900, flow: "row",  share: { logo: 15, nav: 55, actions: 30 } },
            { from: 600, flow: "row",  share: { logo: 20, nav: 80, actions: 0 } },
            { from: 0,   flow: "stack" },
        ] } ],
        logo:    Logo    [ ],
        nav:     Nav     [ ],
        actions: Actions [ ],
    ]

Each entry's `from` means *use this plan when the view is at least this wide*
— the entry with the largest `from` that fits wins, wherever it sits in the
list, and an entry with `from: 0` is the fallback for anything narrower.
`flow` is the arrangement: `"row"` places children left to right; `"stack"`
places them top to bottom. `share` divides the width (what is left of it
after the gaps) among the children it names — the names are the view's own
child names, checked when the layout first arranges (a name with no child is
a loud error). `logo: 15` gives logo 15% of it; **`0` hides that child while
the plan is active** — so "the actions disappear on small screens" is just a
number in the narrow plan, and they reappear by themselves when the view
widens. A child a plan does not name is left alone: natural width, the flow
just places it. `gap` sets the space between children (an entry may carry
its own `gap` to override the layout's). Heights are never touched: children
keep their own heights, and the view's height falls out of its content, as
always.

So the example reads as a storyboard: at 900 and up, a three-across row split
15/55/30; between 600 and 900, the actions drop and the nav takes their room;
below 600, everything stacks.

**Slack and alignment.** When a row's children keep natural widths, the run
may not fill the view — and where the run sits is said with structure, not a
knob: a `Spacer [ ]` child absorbs the slack. Between two groups it pushes
them apart; one on each side centers the run; one first right-aligns it. On
the axis the flow does not manage, a child places itself with the ordinary
literals (`y = center` in a row). Shares that fill the width leave no slack
at all — *shares fill; naturals align.*

**Nesting — who decides what.** A ResponsiveLayout watches its own view's
width — not the window's. The parent's plan decides how much room each child
gets; each child decides what to do with the room it got — if the child has
its own ResponsiveLayout, its plans answer to its own width, automatically.
Room flows down; each level responds locally. (A plan can only name direct
children — managing a grandchild is the child's own plan's business.)

**Division of labor.** ResponsiveLayout manages **named regions**. A collection
of uniform, replicated cards that should reflow to fit is the other tool:
`WrappingLayout` (it wraps by fitting, no plan needed) with a width
constraint on the card.

**When the rules aren't enough.** A plan speaks width, flow, share, and gap.
Whole alternate configurations beyond geometry are a `State` applied on a
width condition; fully custom geometry is a subclass overriding `place()` —
the same seam every layout in the library is built on.

tree.name: Spacer
tree.doc:
When a row (or stack) does not fill its container, the leftover space has to
go somewhere — and the laid children cannot take it themselves (their
flow-axis slot is owned by the layout). A Spacer says where, structurally: put one between two
groups and they push apart ("logo left, actions right"); put one on each
side of a run and it centers; put one first and the run right-aligns.
Several spacers split the slack evenly. When there is no slack — a plan
whose shares fill the width, an auto-sized container — a Spacer is simply
zero and invisible in effect.

The layout owns a Spacer's flow-axis size (a percent-family constraint, so
a container deriving its extent from its children never counts one); the
`flexes` marker is what a flow layout looks for. An empty view otherwise —
it paints nothing and has no size of its own.

tree.name: Table
tree.doc:
The list collection, componentized: the selection-bearing, scroll-owning frame around a replicated (or
written) collection, carrying the selection model so no app hand-rolls it again:

- **Selection is the Table's value** — `selected` (the primary member) and
  `selection` (all of them, presented order), holding **members**: the record
  for a replicated row, the row view itself for a written one. App-ownable via
  `input`; identity by the usual ladder (a record's `id` by convention, else
  the object itself — the reconciler's own rule).
- **The three facts**: selection, the anchor (where ranges extend from), and
  the keyboard position `active` — moved by arrows, extended by shift,
  walked alone by ⌘ with Space toggling (discontiguous keyboard selection).
- **`selects` declares the mode**: `none | single | multi` (default single).
- Rows are TableRow instances — the RadioGroup discipline: direct children
  reaching their table as `parent`, replicated over data or written by hand.
  The row template stays free of any selection wiring.
- Windowing composes: put `virtualize` on the row template and selection,
  ranges, and keyboard travel keep working — members are read from the data
  through any row's cursor, never from instances, so an unmaterialized row
  can be range-selected and arrow travel scrolls it into existence (rows are
  assumed uniform in height).

    Table [ width = 300, height = 400, datapath = { app.d.value },
        selects = "multi", input(sel: object) { app.chosen = sel },
        TableRow [ datapath = :rows[], height = 30,
            t: TextLabel [ x = 8, text = :label ] ] ]

```declare
App [ width = 320, height = 200,
    d: Dataset { { "rows": [ { "id": 1, "label": "Ada" },
                             { "id": 2, "label": "Grace" },
                             { "id": 3, "label": "Alan" } ] } },
    t: Table [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 200, height = 100, datapath = { d.value },
        selects = "multi",
        TableRow [ datapath = :rows[], height = 26,
            Text [ x = 8, y = center, text = :label ]
            ]
        ],
    Text [ x = 20, y = 140, text = { (t.selection ?? []).length + " selected" } ]
    ]
```

filters, and windowing** because it was never a set of instances.

The list collection, componentized: the selection-bearing, scroll-owning frame around a replicated (or
written) collection, carrying the selection model so no app hand-rolls it again:

- **Selection is the Table's value** — `selected` (the primary member) and
  `selection` (all of them, presented order), holding **members**: the record
  for a replicated row, the row view itself for a written one. App-ownable via
  `input`; identity by the usual ladder (a record's `id` by convention, else
  the object itself — the reconciler's own rule).

  the keyboard position `active` — moved by arrows, extended by shift,
  walked alone by ⌘ with Space toggling (discontiguous keyboard selection).
- **`selects` declares the mode**: `none | single | multi` (default single).
- Rows are TableRow instances — the RadioGroup discipline: direct children
  reaching their table as `parent`, replicated over data or written by hand.
  The row template stays free of any selection wiring.
- Windowing composes: put `virtualize` on the row template and selection,
  ranges, and keyboard travel keep working — members are read from the data
  through any row's cursor, never from instances, so an unmaterialized row
  can be range-selected and arrow travel scrolls it into existence (rows are
  assumed uniform in height).

tree.name: Combobox
tree.doc:
Filter-as-you-type over a collection: a text field owning a **query** plus a
dismissable option list owning a **choice** — a derived selection over data.
Composition, not invention: `TextInput` for the entry, the `Menu` machinery for
the list (overlay, raise, light-dismiss, Escape closes — the whole dismissal
discipline rides along), and the matches are a derived collection — a
constraint over the items array, so the live match count is free and no
rendered row is ever scanned.

    Combobox [ width = 240, placeholder = "Assignee",
        items = { app.people }, input(v: object) { app.assignee = v } ]

- **Items are members** (the selection model's currency): records — shown by
  their `label` (or `id`) — or plain strings. `value` holds the chosen member;
  `input(v)` is the delivery seam: the default writes `value`, a use-site
  override redirects and the slot stays untouched.
- **Typing filters live** (case-insensitive substring); opening without typing
  shows the full list (the disclosure-button path). Picking echoes the label
  into the field and closes; editing again re-filters from the new text.
- **Keyboard**: arrows rove the list (the Menu rover), Enter picks the roved
  row — or the first match when none is roved (the type-then-Enter path);
  Escape closes the list (then a second Escape leaves the control — the
  focus-scope ascent). The list is never a tab stop of its own.
- The list is a collection like any other — bind 100k options and
  `virtualize` applies to it the same way (via the Menu it composes).

```declare
App [ width = 320, height = 160, picked: string = "",
    people: array = { ["Ada Lovelace", "Grace Hopper", "Alan Turing", "Barbara Liskov"] },
    Combobox [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 240, placeholder = "Assignee",
        items = { app.people },
        input(v: object) { app.picked = "" + v }
        ],
    Text [ x = 20, y = 80, text = { app.picked == "" ? "—" : app.picked } ]
    ]
```

tree.name: ContextMenu
tree.doc:
The right-click / long-press menu: `Menu`'s machinery whole — overlay, raise,
pointer-anchored placement with viewport clamping, the Mac light-dismiss rule
(an outside press closes **and** is swallowed), Escape closes the chain — with
a gesture-opened entry. It has no overlay machinery of its own; whatever it
does, `Menu` does.

Declared once, opened by many. **The serving view declares the gesture** — that
declaration is what routes it (the claim model: `contextMenu` engages the
right-click/two-finger path, `hold` is the touch long-press gate, and each
engages only where a handler is declared). The whole wiring is two lines on
the view the menu serves:

    rowMenu: ContextMenu [ items = { … }, picked(id: string) { … } ],
    …
    Row [ …,
        onContextMenu(e: PointerEvent) { app.rowMenu.open(this, e) },
        onHold(e: PointerEvent) { app.rowMenu.open(this, e) } ]

`open(v, e)` anchors at the pointer (view-relative event coordinates walked to
root space) and clamps inside the app — Menu's own placement discipline. Items
are the standard Menu records — written lists or derived from the opener
(`items = { … opener … }` for per-row menus with zero per-row instances);
picking delivers through `picked(id)` and closes.

Everything else — `items`, `opener`, `picked`, the rover, the cascade, dismissal — is
`Menu`'s, documented there.

```declare
App [ width = 320, height = 130, chose: string = "",
    rowMenu: ContextMenu [ items = { [ ({ id: "open", label: "Open" }),
                                      ({ id: "rename", label: "Rename" }),
                                      ({ divider: true }),
                                      ({ id: "delete", label: "Delete" }) ] },
        picked(id: string) { app.chose = id }
        ],
    card: View [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 200, height = 44, cornerRadius = 8, fill = darkslategray,
        onContextMenu(e: PointerEvent) { app.rowMenu.open(this, e) },
        onHold(e: PointerEvent) { app.rowMenu.open(this, e) },
        Text [ x = 12, y = center, text = "Right-click or hold me" ]
        ],
    Text [ x = 20, y = 80, text = { app.chose == "" ? "—" : app.chose } ]
    ]
```

tree.name: DataGrid
tree.doc:
The Table contract plus a **column model**: headers, sortable, reorderable and
resizable by drag, touch-correct, over a windowed collection.

    DataGrid [ width = 600, height = 400, datapath = { app.d.value },
        selects = "multi",
        Column [ title = "ID",    field = "id",    width = 70 ],
        Column [ title = "Title", field = "title", width = 280 ],
        Column [ title = "State", field = "state", width = 110 ],
        GridRow [ datapath = :rows[], virtualize = true ] ]

- **Columns are written members** (`Column`: permanent, authored, its identity
  the child itself): `title` heads the column, `field` names what a cell
  shows, `width` is the authored width — a plain value (the column model
  derives through an unanalyzed children walk; a responsive width belongs in
  the grid's `widths` state, which is a tracked dependency:
  `widths = { app.narrow ? ({ id: 40, … }) : null }`). A column's id is its
  `field` (title as fallback).
- **Order and widths are the grid's value-pattern state**: `order` (column
  ids, presented order) and `widths` (id → width overrides). Reorder delivers
  through `arrangeInput(order)`, resize through `resizeInput(id, w)` — the
  defaults write the slots; an app override owns them (persisted layouts).
  Widths are plain values — nothing measures cells.
- **Header interactions**: click sorts — a delivery (`sortInput(on, dir)`,
  writing `sortOn`/`sortDir` by default): sort names a derivation, the truth
  stays in data (the app derives the sorted dataset; a grid displays the
  order its collection has). Horizontal drag reorders (the new order commits
  on release); the right-edge grip resizes. Both drags declare `claim = x` —
  on touch the page keeps vertical pan while the drag owns x.
- **Rows**: the use site writes one bare `GridRow` template over its rows
  path — cells generate from the column model, each showing `record[field]`.
  Selection, keyboard, windowing: Table's, unchanged — `virtualize` on the
  template windows the grid, and the header (a preceding sibling) offsets
  the window's geometry.
- Focus: the grid lands as one tab stop, in browse mode — arrows navigate
  rows.
- Narrow widths: a cell clips; a `widths` entry of `0` drops its column
  entirely — priority, not squish.

Selection, keyboard travel and windowing are `Table`'s, documented there. What follows
is only the column model.

```declare
App [ width = 440, height = 220,
    d: Dataset { { "rows": [ { "id": 1, "title": "Fix the rail",      "state": "open" },
                             { "id": 2, "title": "Draft the chapter", "state": "done" },
                             { "id": 3, "title": "Measure the grid",  "state": "open" } ] } },
    DataGrid [ x = 20, y = 50, width = 400, height = 130, datapath = { d.value },
        selects = "multi",
        Column [ title = "ID",    field = "id",    width = 50 ],
        Column [ title = "Title", field = "title", width = 220 ],
        Column [ title = "State", field = "state", width = 110 ],
        GridRow [ datapath = :rows[] ]
        ]
    ]
```

click a header to sort.

attributes.name: escaped

tree.name: Column
tree.doc:
The Table contract plus a **column model**: headers, sortable, reorderable and
resizable by drag, touch-correct, over a windowed collection.

    DataGrid [ width = 600, height = 400, datapath = { app.d.value },
        selects = "multi",
        Column [ title = "ID",    field = "id",    width = 70 ],
        Column [ title = "Title", field = "title", width = 280 ],
        Column [ title = "State", field = "state", width = 110 ],
        GridRow [ datapath = :rows[], virtualize = true ] ]

- **Columns are written members** (`Column`: permanent, authored, its identity
  the child itself): `title` heads the column, `field` names what a cell
  shows, `width` is the authored width — a plain value (the column model
  derives through an unanalyzed children walk; a responsive width belongs in
  the grid's `widths` state, which is a tracked dependency:
  `widths = { app.narrow ? ({ id: 40, … }) : null }`). A column's id is its
  `field` (title as fallback).
- **Order and widths are the grid's value-pattern state**: `order` (column
  ids, presented order) and `widths` (id → width overrides). Reorder delivers
  through `arrangeInput(order)`, resize through `resizeInput(id, w)` — the
  defaults write the slots; an app override owns them (persisted layouts).
  Widths are plain values — nothing measures cells.
- **Header interactions**: click sorts — a delivery (`sortInput(on, dir)`,
  writing `sortOn`/`sortDir` by default): sort names a derivation, the truth
  stays in data (the app derives the sorted dataset; a grid displays the
  order its collection has). Horizontal drag reorders (the new order commits
  on release); the right-edge grip resizes. Both drags declare `claim = x` —
  on touch the page keeps vertical pan while the drag owns x.
- **Rows**: the use site writes one bare `GridRow` template over its rows
  path — cells generate from the column model, each showing `record[field]`.
  Selection, keyboard, windowing: Table's, unchanged — `virtualize` on the
  template windows the grid, and the header (a preceding sibling) offsets
  the window's geometry.
- Focus: the grid lands as one tab stop, in browse mode — arrows navigate
  rows.
- Narrow widths: a cell clips; a `widths` entry of `0` drops its column
  entirely — priority, not squish.

Selection, keyboard travel and windowing are `Table`'s, documented there. What follows
is only the column model.

```declare
App [ width = 440, height = 220,
    d: Dataset { { "rows": [ { "id": 1, "title": "Fix the rail",      "state": "open" },
                             { "id": 2, "title": "Draft the chapter", "state": "done" },
                             { "id": 3, "title": "Measure the grid",  "state": "open" } ] } },
    DataGrid [ x = 20, y = 50, width = 400, height = 130, datapath = { d.value },
        selects = "multi",
        Column [ title = "ID",    field = "id",    width = 50 ],
        Column [ title = "Title", field = "title", width = 220 ],
        Column [ title = "State", field = "state", width = 110 ],
        GridRow [ datapath = :rows[] ]
        ]
    ]
```

click a header to sort.

tree.name: Segmented
tree.doc:
A row of mutually exclusive choices — the control you reach for when the options
are few, named, and worth showing all at once. Its choices are **data**, like
`Menu`'s items and `DataGrid`'s columns:

```declare-fragment
Segmented [ width = 300, value = { app.page },
    choices = { [ ({ id: "controls", label: "Controls" }),
                 ({ id: "table",    label: "Table" }),
                 ({ id: "grid",     label: "DataGrid" }) ] },
    input(v: object) { app.page = "" + v }
    ]
```

### Why data, and not `Segment` children

Because the sliding highlight cannot be built any other way. The pill has to know
which choice is selected and how wide each one is, and a constraint may not ask
the view tree that: `childViews` carries **set membership only**, so `.length` is
live while anything reaching into the collection is refused —
`aggregation over a reactive node collection … derive from data [DECLARE7001]`.
The compiler names the answer.

### Equal widths — a choice, not a limitation

Segments divide the control's width evenly. This is a design decision and it
could be otherwise: a `Layout`'s `place()` may aggregate over children — that is
how `SimpleLayout` sizes a variable-width row — so a strategy that placed each
segment by its own label and interpolated the pill between neighbours is
buildable. The `DECLARE7001` refusal binds constraints reaching into the view
tree, not the layout strategy whose job that is. Three reasons not to:

- **A segmented control divides evenly; a row of buttons sizes to content.** The
  two are different controls, and this one is the first.
- **The segmented convention makes it a content rule**: keep segment labels short and
  similar in length. Equal width enforces that rather than tolerating it. One long
  label makes the whole control look wrong, which is the feedback you want.
- **The sliding pill.** At equal widths it translates at constant width. At
  variable widths it would have to morph its width while travelling, which reads
  as rubbery and worsens the more the labels differ. Most platforms never meet
  this, because their highlight pops.

The cost is real and worth stating plainly: **a `Segmented` does not self-size to
its labels.** Set `width`, or accept `segMin × choices.length`.

### The pill

The highlight springs a **normalized lane** — a float index — not pixels. `x` is
then `lane × segW`, so a resize recomputes `segW` and the pill **snaps** to the
right place instead of skating across the bar on every layout change. The chosen
segment wears a raised `surface` pill with a hairline.

```declare
App [ width = 340, height = 130, page: string = "one",
    Segmented [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 300, value = { app.page },
        choices = { [ ({ id: "one", label: "One" }),
                     ({ id: "two", label: "Two" }),
                     ({ id: "three", label: "Three" }) ] },
        input(v: object) { app.page = "" + v }
        ],
    Text [ x = 20, y = 74, text = { "showing: " + app.page } ]
    ]
```

tree.name: Icon
tree.doc:
A small monochrome mark, **drawn** rather than typed. A font's glyphs are not
marks: they are not guaranteed to be present, they rasterize differently on
every platform, and the ones that exist are the wrong shapes — a `✓` sits on the
text baseline and reads like a square-root sign, not like a checkmark. The
library's own marks — `Checkbox.mark`, `Menu.check`, the `Combobox` disclosure —
are all `Icon`s.

### Writing one

Subclass and override `draw`. Author the shape in a **16×16 box** — `unit`
converts it to whatever size the host asked for:

```declare-fragment
class SparkIcon extends Icon [
    draw(d: Draw) {
        d.scale(unit, unit)
        d.strokeStyle = ink; d.lineWidth = weight / unit
        d.beginPath(); d.moveTo(8, 1); d.lineTo(8, 15); d.stroke()
        }
    ]
```

Overriding a **method** is the refinement path that works — re-opening an
inherited child is not (`cap:` on a `Button` subclass fails at instantiate), so
the shape lives in `draw` and everything adjustable is a slot.

### Size changes the drawing, not the shape

Every icon is **one path**. There are no per-size variants, no thresholds, nothing
redrawn at a breakpoint: `unit` scales the 16-box to whatever the host asked for,
so a 64px icon is the 16px icon at 4×, exactly.

The **stroke** is the deliberate exception. `d.lineWidth = weight / unit` sits
*inside* `d.scale(unit, unit)`, so the two cancel and the line lands at a constant
`weight` in **device pixels at every size**. An icon's line therefore matches the
1px rules and text weights it sits among, instead of fattening as it grows.

The cost is that the stroke-to-size ratio falls: 1.6px is 10% of a 16px icon, 5%
at 32, 2.5% at 64. Across 14–18px — chrome sizes — that is invisible. Past ~32
an icon starts reading as a fine-line drawing rather than a mark — so **this set
is built for chrome sizes**, and a large display icon (an empty-state mark, an
about-box graphic) would want the opposite: `d.lineWidth = weight` *outside* the
scale, so the line grows with the drawing. Real icon systems take a third road
and redraw per optical size range; that is a bigger undertaking than this set
needs.

### What is not an Icon

Application art. The desktop's dock icons are the case to look at before
reaching for this class: they rest at 56px and grow under the magnification
swell, they are polychrome (`gradient(hue1, hue2)` behind a hue-parameterised
drawing), and their **width animates every frame**. Each of those alone rules
them out — the constant stroke that suits a 16px mark is 2.9% of a 56px one and
reads spindly; `ink` is a single colour; and an animated width is the one thing
this set forbids.

The line is not "drawn versus not drawn" — dock art is drawn too. It is
**chrome vocabulary versus identity**. A mark that says *close*, *expand*,
*checked*, *this is the dark theme* belongs here, at a size the host states.
A mark that says *this is Calendar* does not, and belongs to the app that owns
the identity.

Desktop has both, which is what makes it the clarifying example: its menu rows
take `WindowIcon` and `CodeIcon` from this set, while its dock keeps `DockIcon`.

### Two rules

**Scale inside the body, never with the View's `scale`.** A recording rasterizes
into a canvas sized to its own ink bounds at device resolution, while `scale` is
a transform applied *after* — so `scale = { width / 16 }` would rasterize 16
pixels and stretch them. Crisp at exactly 16, soft at every other size, which is
most of them. Scaling inside the recording allocates the raster at true size
instead.

**Never animate an icon's `width`.** Reading size inside `draw` makes the
recording size-dependent: an animated size re-records **and** reallocates the
backing canvas every frame, which drops a magnifying dock of icons from 60 to
~25fps. A static size re-records once and costs nothing after: 120 icons
re-recording their *content* every frame run frame-bound at 16.6ms, cheaper
than the 120 text glyphs they replace.

Colour is not a rule — `ink` follows the provided text colour, so an icon beside
a muted label goes muted on its own, and a host that needs a different ink (a
menu row's check inverting on the hot row) simply sets it.

attributes.name: textColor
attributes.doc:
The effective text colour the mark's `ink` follows — a **provided value**, so an icon

attributes.name: ink
attributes.doc:
The mark's colour. Follows the provided `textColor`, so an icon beside a muted
label goes muted on its own. **The trap: that slot falls back to black platform-wide**,
so an icon in a context that never states a text colour renders black and vanishes on a
dark surface. State `ink` unless you know the context sets one — `IconHost` does it for
every icon built by name.

attributes.name: weight
attributes.doc:
Stroke width in **final device pixels, not authored ones**. Divide by `unit` inside
`draw` (`d.lineWidth = weight / unit`) and the scale cancels, so the line lands at a
constant weight at every size and matches the 1px rules and text it sits among.

constant weight at every size and matches the 1px rules and text it sits among.

attributes.name: unit
attributes.doc:
The 16-box-to-host-size scale factor. **Multiply the path by it; divide the stroke by
it.** Every icon is one path at one size, scaled — there are no per-size variants.

docSegs.md:

attributes.name: width
attributes.doc: Sized by the provided `iconSize`, so a menu states 16 once and every icon in it answers; a use site may set its own.

docSegs.md: Sized by the provided `iconSize`, so a menu states 16 once and every icon in it answers; a use site may set its own.

attributes.name: height
attributes.doc: Square, always — the height follows the width.

example.name: Icon
example.title: Your own mark, drawn once in a 16-box
example.lead: Subclass and override `draw`: author the shape at 16×16, `unit` scales it to the size the host asks for, and the stroke stays a constant `weight` in device pixels. The same path at three sizes, then tinted.
example.source:
class SparkIcon extends Icon [
    draw(d: Draw) {
        d.scale(unit, unit)
        d.strokeStyle = ink; d.lineWidth = weight / unit; d.lineCap = "round"
        d.beginPath(); d.moveTo(8, 1); d.lineTo(8, 15); d.moveTo(1, 8); d.lineTo(15, 8)
        d.moveTo(3.5, 3.5); d.lineTo(12.5, 12.5); d.moveTo(12.5, 3.5); d.lineTo(3.5, 12.5); d.stroke()
        }
    ]


App [ textColor = 0x172530,
    row: View [ x = 20, y = 20, height = 48, width = { this.contentWidth },
        layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = x, spacing = 24 ],   // an Icon centers itself on y
        SparkIcon [ iconSize = 16 ],
        SparkIcon [ iconSize = 24 ],
        SparkIcon [ iconSize = 32 ],
        SparkIcon [ iconSize = 48, ink = 0x2E6FE0 ]
        ]
    ]

tree.name: IconHost
tree.doc:
A control names its icon (`iconLeft = TrashIcon`) rather than nesting one,
   because a control is a leaf and everything else about it is an attribute — and
   because an attribute is the one form where authored and bound are the same
   mechanism. `IconHost` is what turns that name into a live view, through the
   same `app.createView` seam a menu record's `icon` field uses.

   It reserves no space when empty, so a control's `contentWidth` measures only
   the slots that are actually filled and an icon-less button needs no special
   case.

   LIMITATION, deliberate for now: the name is consumed once, at construction.
   A control whose icon must CHANGE at runtime (a play/pause toggle) is not
   served by this yet — that needs a name-valued slot the runtime re-materializes
   on change, which is a runtime feature, not a library one. Every site in this
   corpus names its icon statically.

attributes.name: kind
attributes.doc:
The icon **class name** to build (`"TrashIcon"`). `""` builds nothing and the host
collapses to zero width, so an icon-less control needs no special case. **Consumed once,
at construction** — assigning a new name later does not re-materialize the icon. A name
that is only ever computed needs `use [ Name ]` to survive the build.

example.name: IconHost
example.title: A name becomes a view
example.lead: `kind` names an icon class; the host materializes it through `createView` and reserves no space when the name is empty. It is what lets a control say `iconLeft = "PlusIcon"`.

        layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = x, spacing = 16 ],
        IconHost [ kind = "PlusIcon" ],
        IconHost [ kind = "CheckIcon", ink = 0x12A594 ],
        IconHost [ kind = "CloseIcon", ink = 0xC93B47 ],
        IconHost [ kind = "" ],                              // empty: zero width, nothing reserved
        Text [ textColor = 0x6A7883, text = "← the fourth host is empty and takes no room" ]
        ]
    ]

tree.name: SegmentedItem
tree.doc:
One choice of a `Segmented`, **materialized from that control's `choices` data — never
authored directly**, which is why it carries almost nothing of its own. It is a full
`Control`: its own tab stop, activated by Space or Enter, so a user can tab to an
inactive choice and select it.

It renders rest, hover and press only. **The chosen state is the sliding pill behind
these, not a fill of its own** — which is exactly what lets the pill travel between
segments instead of popping.

attributes.name: location
attributes.doc:
Makes this segment a **real link**: give a choice a `location` and the segment navigates
there in its own `onClick`. This is what keeps a view-switching control visible to link
extraction — the crawler reads `app.location = …` out of activation handlers, and
`input(v)` is not one, since its destination depends on a value that does not exist at
extraction time. Empty for an ordinary segmented control, and an empty read emits no
anchor.

tree.name: ArrowIcon
tree.doc:
An arrow, **not a chevron** — the two mean different things and must not look alike.
A chevron *discloses*; an arrow points at a direction that **is itself the state**:
sort ascending, a trend, a transfer. The shaft is what a chevron lacks. The two often
sit adjacent — a sort-direction control beside a sort-menu popper — and one shape for
both reads as a mistake.

tree.name: SanFrancisco
tree.doc:
Declare's own look — named for where Declare is made — and the theme a widget
renders when nothing provides one: `control.declare` defaults `theme` to
`SanFrancisco` (the light record), so an app that never mentions a theme is San
Francisco light, always. These declarations are the preset itself, written in the
language; the runtime serves them by name.

A record is **complete**, not a delta: every token the standard library consults is
stated, so a preset reads whole with nothing to chase.

segs.md:
# How it ships

Delivery, hosting, and the honest posture — the promises about running and
shipping a Declare program.

### SATOR-1 — Programs are data
A compiled program is data the toolchain can read, so one compiler powers the
documentation system, static extraction for crawlers, and live editing alike —
not three separate pipelines.
*Held in:* FAQ ("programs are data — the same compiler powers the documentation system, static extraction for crawlers, and live editing").

### SATOR-2 — What a visitor sees and what a crawler sees can never drift
Static extraction is built into the compiler: it runs the program headlessly to
its settled state and serializes the actual content as semantic HTML — real
headings, paragraphs, links — baked into the page at build time. A crawler (or an
AI reading the web) reads that; a person gets the live app that replaces it at
boot. No server-side rendering, no hydration — it works on a plain static host.
*Held in:* FAQ ("How do Declare-written sites handle crawlers and SEO"); the "why" essay ("what a visitor sees and what a crawler sees can never drift").

### SATOR-3 — In-browser compilation, and no build step to develop
Because the compiler runs in the page, a page can edit and re-run itself: every
sample is live-editable, and view-source culture is restored. Development needs no
build step — the dev server and the browser use the *same* compiler with
byte-identical output.
*Held in:* FAQ ("What benefits does in-browser compilation bring"); getstarted ("no build step").

### SATOR-4 — You don't ship the compiler
For production, `declarec` precompiles everything into a small, self-contained
artifact — a set of static files you can host anywhere, with no trace of the
toolchain and no compiler aboard.
*Held in:* FAQ ("For production you don't ship the compiler").

### SATOR-5 — The program's URL is the app's address
A program is addressed by its own URL: on the dev server, browse to a `.declare`
file's URL and get the running app. The address is the program, not a route
registered elsewhere.
*Held in:* getstarted ("the program URL is the app's address"); FAQ.

### SATOR-6 — Small, and fast where it counts
A full application ships small — the flagship calendar, application *and* runtime,
at roughly 89 KB gzipped (machine-stamped from
the measured artifact): a compact runtime, practical on a phone over a slow network.
Input latency is low — there is no virtual-DOM pass between gesture and pixels — and
animation runs at the display's full rate. The homepage reports the live size figures,
measured from the deployed artifacts and regenerated with them on every publication.
*Held in:* FAQ ("What should I expect in terms of performance").

### SATOR-7 — Honest about the trades and the gaps
The promises come with their limits stated plainly: a framework with no in-browser
compiler wins the very first cold load (the production path closes the gap by
precompiling); Declare is young and the repository *is* the distribution and the
source of truth; and accessibility depth, an npm package, and a dedicated editor
extension are named, unhidden gaps.
*Held in:* FAQ ("Startup" trade; "How mature is Declare?"; "Is Declare accessible?"; "Is there editor support?").

### SATOR-8 — Open, MIT, entirely public
The complete source — compiler, runtime, standard library, documentation, and the
site itself — is public under the MIT license.
*Held in:* FAQ ("What license is Declare offered under?").

# The wager

Why the language is shaped the way it is: built for the era when much code is
written by machines, and bet on verifiability over familiarity.

### AREPO-1 — Built for machine-written code
When machines write the code, familiarity matters less and *verifiability* matters
more. Declare is designed around that shift, not retrofitted to it.
*Held in:* homepage hero ("a UI language for you and your AI"); FAQ ("Declare is built for the era when much code is written by machines").

### AREPO-2 — The whole language fits in a model's context
The declarative surface is small, closed, and regular — its *entire* definition is
one file (`docs/declare.md`, on the order of 12,000 tokens). No model has
trained on Declare, and none needs to: a model can hold the complete spec while it
writes.
*Held in:* declare.md preamble ("the language, in one file … no LLM has been trained on it"); FAQ; the "why" essay.

### AREPO-3 — Comprehension leverage, not corpus leverage
Declare competes on the kind of leverage a new language *can* have: a language
small enough to hand a model whole, regular enough to be analyzed rather than
pattern-matched, backed by a compiler that turns each mistake into a precise
correction. With less code passing under human eyes, the language and its compiler
are the one reviewer always present.
*Held in:* the "why" essay ("Two kinds of leverage").

### AREPO-4 — Type-checking is mandatory, and trustworthy
Every `{ }` body is type-checked on every compile, with no opt-out, and the
checker is held to **zero false positives** across the repository's own corpus —
every app, component, and doc example it ships. So an error always means something
is genuinely wrong.
*Held in:* FAQ ("Mandatory type-checking … zero false positives").

### AREPO-5 — Diagnostics name the fix
A compiler message is written to steer the *next* attempt — it states the rule and
names the rewrite that fixes it, including "did you mean" guidance for instincts
carried from other frameworks. The primary reader of a diagnostic, now, is a model
deciding what to do next.
*Held in:* FAQ ("Diagnostics that name the fix"); the "why" essay.

### AREPO-6 — No magic
Declare consistently chooses predictability over cleverness: dependencies are
extracted statically, events don't bubble, there is one way to say most things.
Where it looks familiar it behaves as you'd assume; where it is genuinely new it
*looks* new — a cue to consult the spec rather than autocomplete from memory.
*Held in:* FAQ ("No magic"); the "why" essay.

### AREPO-7 — Tested against models, not assumed
The claim that Declare suits LLMs is tested: an evaluation harness gives
model tiers application-building tasks cold, one-shot and iterated, and failures
feed back into the language, the diagnostics, and the docs. The documentation
doubles as training material — every code fence in the teaching docs is
compiled by the test suite, so nothing a model reads is stale or wrong.
*Held in:* FAQ ("What has been done during Declare's development to optimize for LLM usage").

### AREPO-8 — The human owns intent; the toolchain keeps the text honest
The workflow the language is designed around: a person directs and reviews; a
model writes the text; the compiler stays in the loop. The flagship calendar
reports its own number — zero lines written by hand.
*Held in:* FAQ ("The calendar says '0 lines written by hand'").

# The standing model

Reactivity and continuity — the central idea the whole language is arranged
around.

### TENET-1 — A binding is a standing relationship the runtime keeps true
Read a reactive value inside a binding and you are subscribed; assign to one and
everything bound to it updates. That is the defining idea, and it holds with no
re-render, no diffing, no dependency array, and no hook — the relationship is
kept true for you, not re-run by you.
*Held in:* declare.md §1.

### TENET-2 — Reactivity is derived by the compiler, not guessed at runtime
The compiler works out what every binding depends on, statically. Behavior is
therefore predictable and analyzable by tools rather than discovered as the
program runs — the model reasons about exactly what the compiler verifies.
*Held in:* FAQ ("reactivity is *derived by the compiler*, not guessed at runtime"); the "why" essay.

### TENET-3 — Continuity is the grain, not the garnish
Layout, states, springs, and data all derive from the same constraints, so a view
doesn't switch so much as *become* the next one — and the continuous version of
an interface is often *less* code than the discrete one. The prized, usually
bespoke layer of UX moves into the declarative, analyzable layer.
*Held in:* README ("continuity is the grain, not the garnish"); the "why" essay ("Declare makes continuity the grain, not the garnish").

### TENET-4 — Motion, layout, and modes are all just values
Motion is physics on an attribute — a `Spring` toward where a thing belongs, with
interruption just the target changing. Layout is a reactive slot you can swap,
derive, or animate. A mode is a reversible bundle of overrides that cannot leak,
so modes compose and interrupt cleanly.
*Held in:* declare.md §1, §5, §8.

### TENET-5 — State derives from data and location, not from control flow
Screens follow data state (`shown = { data.loaded }`), not navigation code. There
is no router object: `location` is an attribute wired to the URL fragment, and
state *derives* from it the same way everything else derives — a deep link is
just an initial value.
*Held in:* declare.md §7; FAQ ("There's no router object — location is an attribute, like everything else").

# How you write it

The shape of the language and how programs compose — the promises about the
authoring surface.

### OPERA-1 — Two delimiters carry the whole model
`[ … ]` is the view tree — a component's attributes, children, and declarations,
its bracket nesting *being* the tree. `{ … }` is TypeScript — a value, a handler
body, a script. Those two are the entire mental model.
*Held in:* declare.md §2; getstarted ("Two delimiters carry the whole model").

### OPERA-2 — All real logic is ordinary TypeScript
Everything inside `{ }` is ordinary TypeScript — no new expression language to
learn — type-checked with full knowledge of every component's attributes. What
you (or a model) already know about TypeScript carries over — at full expression
strength; type annotations and declarations live on attributes, not in bodies.
*Held in:* README ("with all real logic in ordinary TypeScript"); FAQ ("There is no new expression language to learn").

### OPERA-3 — No CSS, by design
Styling is part of the language: paint attributes on views, theme records that
reskin a whole subtree from one place, named style bundles switched at runtime.
No cascade, no specificity, no selectors. CSS *knowledge* transfers — colors,
font stacks, shadows read the same — but there is no stylesheet, which is also
what makes a non-DOM renderer possible.
*Held in:* FAQ ("Can I use CSS to style a Declare app? No — and that's a feature").

### OPERA-4 — Values derive down, information travels up, internals stay private
A component is a class; its attributes are its public interface, and values
*derive down* through constraints. Information travels back *up* through events a
component declares and fires — delivered to the handler that declared interest,
never bubbled through the tree. Inside, code reaches other parts only through
explicit scopes (`this`, `parent`, `classroot`, `app`), so a component's
internals stay its own.
*Held in:* FAQ ("How do encapsulation and composition work"); declare.md.

### OPERA-5 — The library is written in Declare, with no privileged API
The entire standard library is written in Declare itself, in readable source you
can open and live-edit. There is no privileged component API underneath: library
components are the same kind of thing your components are, used identically —
including replication over data.
*Held in:* FAQ ("How are Declare's UI components created?").

### OPERA-6 — Data binds declaratively
Data enters the way everything else does: a `Dataset` or fetched `DataSource`, a
`datapath` cursor whose descendants read relative to it, replication per element
of a bound array, and two-way binding for editable fields. Large collections can declare a
windowed materialization (`virtualize`, opt-in) rather than building everything.
*Held in:* FAQ ("How do I get data into an app?").

# What Declare is

The nature of the thing — the promises about what kind of language it is.

### ROTAS-1 — A language, not a framework
Declare is a domain-specific language for user interfaces — the way SQL is a DSL
for queries — not a library inside JavaScript. There is no framework runtime to
orchestrate, no lifecycle to manage.
*Held in:* homepage hero; FAQ ("It's a language, not a framework inside JavaScript").

### ROTAS-2 — The UI is a standing structure, not a re-run function
An interface is a standing tree that values flow through when things change —
never a function the platform re-runs and diffs. There is no re-render, no
virtual-DOM pass, no reconciliation.
*Held in:* declare.md §1 ("A binding is a relationship, not a callback … standing expressions the runtime keeps true"); FAQ ("the UI is a *standing structure* … nothing re-renders because nothing was ever a render").

### ROTAS-3 — One program, any renderer
One source tree renders to managed DOM or directly to pixels on a canvas — and
runs headlessly, no screen at all — with the same layout and input handling. The
language owns its semantics; no DOM assumptions leak into a program. The DOM and
canvas renderers are held equal, verified pixel-for-pixel, and the native Mac host is held
to both by a conformance suite. (The Mac host is a renderer, first-class and complete for
what it does; it is not yet a way to deliver an offline desktop application, which needs
integration the host does not have.)
*Held in:* FAQ ("renderer-independence"); the guide's Renderers chapter.

### ROTAS-4 — One tree, one language
Structure, style, and behavior are one tree in one language — not the HTML/CSS/JS
trinity. There is no separate stylesheet, template, and script to keep in sync.
*Held in:* FAQ ("There is also no HTML/CSS/JS trinity — structure, style, and behavior are one tree in one language").

### ROTAS-5 — Compiled, everywhere
Declare is a compiled language, and the compiler runs anywhere the program does —
in Node and in the browser, the same compiler with byte-identical output.
*Held in:* FAQ ("The compiler itself runs anywhere — in Node, or in the browser"); declare.md §1.

### ROTAS-6 — A successor that kept the convictions
Declare is a from-the-ground-up successor to OpenLaszlo (2002): it keeps the
declarative tree, constraint-based reactivity, and a real compiler, and rebuilds
everything else — keyword-free syntax, TypeScript for logic, DOM and canvas
renderers, in-browser compilation — for the modern, LLM era.
*Held in:* FAQ ("Where does Declare come from?").

forms.name: schema

app.name: App [ … ]
app.lead:
A program is one tree, and `App [ … ]` is its root — one per program. With `width` and
`height` unset it fills its host, which is the common case: the page, the window, the
island it is mounted in. Everything else nests inside its brackets, and `app` (lower case)
names the running instance from any depth, so application-wide state belongs here.

Any instance may declare its own members, the App included — attributes, methods,
handlers, children — with no class at all; the compiler synthesizes an anonymous subclass.
The top-level forms (`class`, `include`, `use`, `script`, `font`, `style`, `theme`,
`schema`) may come before or after it, in any order.

example.name: form-app
example.title: The one root
example.lead: `App [ … ]` fills its host when its size is unset. It may declare members of its own — a fact here, read by a text below through `app`, the instance's name from any depth.

App [ fill = 0xF6F8FA, textColor = 0x172530, fontSize = 14,
    visits: number = 0,
    onClick() { visits = visits + 1 },
    Text [ x = 20, y = 20, text = { "the app is " + app.width + " × " + app.height + " — click anywhere" } ],
    deep: View [ x = 20, y = 50,
        Text [ text = { "clicks reach the root's fact: " + app.visits } ]
        ]
    ]

instance.name: Type [ … ]
instance.lead:
Square brackets hold a component's members — attributes, declarations, methods, handlers,
children — and the nesting of brackets *is* the tree. Naming a type with a bracketed body
instantiates it: `Text [ text = "OK" ]` is a Text, `bg: View [ … ]` a View reachable as `bg`.
Every member inside is one of the five shapes (set, declare, child, method, handler),
separated by commas.

An instance is a full component in its own right: it may declare new attributes and methods
without a class, because the compiler synthesizes an anonymous subclass for it. Promote a
one-off to a named `class` when you instantiate it twice, or need to name its type.

example.name: form-instance
example.title: Brackets are the tree

class.lead:
A component is a class, and this is the one way to define one. Everything inside the
brackets is a **member**: `name = value` sets an attribute the base already has,
`name: Type = value` declares a new one, `name: Type [ … ]` is a named child, `name() { … }`
a method, `onThing() { … }` a handler for an event the node fires. Instantiate the class by
naming it with a `[ ]` body, as many times as you like; each instance may set any attribute
and add members of its own.

A class is not a file and not a module. It is a top-level declaration, and a program is one
tree of them — `include` merges another file's classes into the same program, and there is
nothing to export. Any instance may declare members with no class at all, because the
compiler synthesizes an anonymous subclass; promote a one-off to a named class when you
instantiate it twice, or when you need to name its type.

example.name: form-class
example.title: Declare once, instantiate by name
example.lead: A `Chip` with a declared attribute, a derived width, a handler, and a child. Three instances; the third re-sets `fill` at its use site, which any instance may do with any attribute.
example.source:
class Chip extends View [ height = 30, cornerRadius = 10, fill = { hovered ? 0x4682B4 : 0x2F4F4F },
    label: string = "",
    picks: number = 0,
    width = { this.t.width + 20 },
    onClick() { picks = picks + 1 },
    t: Text [ x = 10, y = 7, fontSize = 13, textColor = white,
        text = { picks == 0 ? label : label + " ×" + picks } ]
    ]


App [
    row: View [ x = 20, y = 20, height = 30, width = { this.contentWidth },
        layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = x, spacing = 10 ],
        Chip [ label = "one" ],
        Chip [ label = "two" ],
        Chip [ label = "three", fill = firebrick ]     // a use site re-sets an attribute
        ]
    ]

example.name: form-classroot
example.title: Reaching the component from inside it
example.lead: `classroot` is the instance itself from any depth in the class body — here a click on the header selects the tab, and the caption reads the tab's label. `this` in that handler would be the header.
example.source:
class Tab extends View [ width = 120, height = 36, cornerRadius = [8, 8, 0, 0],
    selected: boolean = false,
    label: string = "",
    fill = { selected ? 0xFFFFFF : 0xDCDCDC },
    select() { selected = !selected },
    header: View [ width = { parent.width }, height = { parent.height },
        onClick() { classroot.select() },                 // `this` here is the header, not the tab
        caption: Text [ x = 12, y = 9, fontSize = 14, text = { classroot.label } ]
        ]
    ]


App [ fill = 0xEEF1F4,
    row: View [ x = 20, y = 20, height = 36, width = { this.contentWidth },
        layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = x, spacing = 4 ],
        Tab [ label = "Inbox", selected = true ],
        Tab [ label = "Sent" ],
        Tab [ label = "Drafts" ]
        ]
    ]

extends.name: extends
extends.lead:
Single inheritance from another component — a library class or one of your own. The
subclass sees every attribute, child, method, and event of the base. Re-stating an
attribute with `name = value` **overrides** its default; re-stating a method replaces it;
and a base's named child is reached by name, not redeclared. Omit `extends` altogether and
the base is `View`.

`extends` is not a top-level form in its own right: it is part of a `class` declaration.
The base may be declared later in the file, or in an included one. What a subclass may
extend is what the runtime can wire: `View`, `Node`, `Layout` (and `TweenLayout`), and any
class descending from them.

declares** is one real view of that class, placed in the flowing line as an atomic box the
words wrap around. There is no whitelist to extend and no attribute to set: the class
existing is what makes the tag mean it, matched by the name exactly as written, in both
formats (`HTMLText`'s `html` and `Markdown`'s `text`). A tag naming no class of yours keeps
the meaning it already had — the HTML whitelist, an autolink, a literal `<` — and a
`<span class>` stays a style, never a view.

The tag's attributes are the class's, each converted from its string by the slot's
**declared** type, exactly as a source literal is: `id='142'` is the number in a `number`
slot, `tint='#DDF4E4'` a `Color`, `align='center'` an enum member, `width='50%'` a percent of
the width the text flows in, a bare `hot` is `true`. The tag **is the use site**, so an
attribute takes use-site precedence over what the class body sets for that slot — a literal
or a `{ }` constraint — and only the winner installs; a slot the tag does not mention keeps
the class's own behaviour. `x`/`y` are refused — the flow places the view, as a layout places
its children — and an unknown attribute, a value that will not convert, a read-only slot, or
a percent on a slot with no axis goes to the component's `unsupported` policy. The view owns
its `width`/`height` while the flow owns its `x`/`y`, it never splits
across a line, a taller one grows its line, a size change re-flows the text, and it reads the
surrounding run's text face as provided values. Content is reactive: a tag still present keeps
its view and its state, with only changed attributes rewritten (a tag that gains or loses an
attribute is built again, since what it claims is settled at build), and `key='…'` fixes that
identity when the order moves. Markup carries no expressions, so a live value is either
concatenated into the content (with `escapeHtml` around every interpolated value) or derived
inside the class from an identity the content names.

example.name: form-inlineview
example.title: A view in the middle of a sentence
example.lead: A tag whose name is a class this program declares builds one real view of that class, placed in the flowing line as an atomic box the words wrap around. Each chip sizes itself to its label and carries its own state — click one and watch the line re-flow around its new width, which no styled run of text could do.
example.source:
class Chip extends View [
    label: string = "",
    picked: boolean = false,
    height = 20, width = { this.t.width + 20 }, cornerRadius = 10,
    fill = { picked ? 0x4C8DFF : (hovered ? 0xDDE4EB : 0xE9EEF3) },
    onClick() { picked = !picked },
    t: TextLabel [ x = 10, y = center, fontSize = 12, fontWeight = medium,
        text = { classroot.picked ? classroot.label + " ✓" : classroot.label },
        textColor = { classroot.picked ? 0xFFFFFF : 0x33424E } ]
    ]


App [ fill = #F6F8FA, textColor = 0x172530, fontSize = 15,
    HTMLText [ x = 20, y = 18, width = 420, lineHeight = 1.45, bodyColor = 0x33424E,
        html = "Filed under <Chip label='docs'/>, <Chip label='runtime'/> and <Chip label='renderers'/> — every chip here is a view, with a size of its own, a state of its own, and the whole language available to it." ]

set.name: name = value
set.lead:
Sets an attribute the component already has. The right-hand side is one of three things,
and the spelling says which: a **bare literal** (a number, a percent, a color, a string, a
keyword — set once), a **`{ }` constraint** (TypeScript that stays true), or a **`:path`**
read from bound data. A bare `[ … ]` list fills an array-typed slot.

One family of names may be set on a component that does not declare them: the built-in
**provided values** — the text face (`fontSize`, `fontFamily`, `fontWeight`, `textColor`,
`letterSpacing`), `theme`, `iconSize`, and the rich-text slots. Setting one on a container
*provides* it to every descendant that reads it (see `provided`).

A set attribute with a `{ }` **owns a cell**: the runtime keeps it current, and a direct
write to it is refused with a message naming the fix — derived state is never assigned;
change its inputs. In a handler, `name = value` is the setter: the write lands when the
handler returns, together with every other write it made, in one settle.

rules.rule: The attribute must exist on the component — to introduce a new one, declare it with a type.
rules.says: App has no attribute 'widht' — did you mean 'width'?

rules.rule: A bare value must be of the slot's kind; the message names the vocabulary the slot takes.
rules.says: App.width expects a Length (a number of pixels, a percent like 50%, or the position literals center | end on x/y), got the string "ten"

rules.says: got 'W' — write { W } to bind the attribute

script { const W = 10 }
App [ width = W ]

rules.rule: A list belongs to an array-typed slot; a scalar slot refuses one.
rules.says: got the list […, …]

example.name: form-set
example.title: Three ways to set one attribute
example.lead: A bare literal is set once; a `{ }` stays true; a `:path` reads bound data. Drag the slider: the second box follows it, the first never moves, the third reads a record.

declare.name: name: Type = value
syntax: name: Type                                 // no default: undefined until written
panel: Menu = null                         // a component class — the slot holds an instance
declare.syntaxText:
name: Type = value
name: Type                                 // no default: undefined until written
rows: Row[] = []
panel: Menu = null                         // a component class — the slot holds an instance
declare.lead:
Declares a new reactive attribute — the way state enters a program. The type comes from the
same vocabulary a signature uses: a primitive (`number`, `string`, `boolean`), `Color`,
`Length`, `Radius`, a component class, a declared schema, a literal union
(`"open" | "closed"`), an array of any of these, or a function type. The default is a bare
literal or a `{ }` expression.

A declaration's `{ }` default is a **formula with no cell**: reading it inlines the
expression, and an assignment simply replaces it — the right tool for a value you may take
over later, which is how `TextInput.initial` differs from its read-only `text = { … }` twin.
Compare `set`: a set attribute's `{ }` owns a cell and refuses assignment.

rules.rule: A declaration carries a type; the colon is not optional.
rules.says: expected a type or component name, got '='

rules.rule: The type must be one the language knows; the message lists them.
rules.says: unknown type 'Widget' — a declared attribute's type is one of number, string, boolean, Color, Length, Radius, Shape, array, object, View, Theme

rules.rule: An attribute the component already has is set, not declared again.
rules.says: App already has an attribute 'width' — a declaration introduces a new one; write 'width = …' to set the existing one

rules.rule: A built-in read-only intrinsic (`hovered`, `pressed`, `dark`, …) is computed for you and cannot be shadowed by a declaration.
rules.says: 'hovered' is a built-in read-only intrinsic of App — it is computed for you; choose another name for your derived value

example.name: form-declare
example.title: Declaring is how state enters
example.lead: Three declared attributes: a number with a literal default, a literal union, and a computed default — a formula with no cell, so an assignment simply replaces it. Click the box to write over the formula; click the reset to put it back.
example.source:
App [ fill = 0xF6F8FA, textColor = 0x172530, fontSize = 14,
    clicks: number = 0,
    mood: "calm" | "busy" = "calm",
    label: string = { mood == "calm" ? "nothing yet" : clicks + " clicks" },   // computed default
    box: View [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 240, height = 44, cornerRadius = 8, fill = 0xE9EFF4,
        onClick() { app.clicks = app.clicks + 1; app.mood = "busy" },
        Text [ x = 12, y = 13, text = { app.label } ]
        ],
    Button [ x = 20, y = 76, label = "write over the formula",
        onClick() { app.label = "written by hand" }
        ],
    Text [ x = 20, y = 118, fontSize = 12, textColor = 0x6A7883,
        text = { "mood: " + app.mood + " · the label is " + (app.label == "written by hand" ? "no longer derived" : "derived") } ]
    ]

child.name: name: Type [ … ]
child.syntaxText:
name: Type [ members ]
Type [ members ]                           // anonymous
child.lead:
A child is a member that is itself an instance. Named, it is reachable from its siblings and
its class as `name`; anonymous, it is placed and painted but never addressed. Children paint
in declaration order — later siblings on top; there is no z-index — and a parent with a
`layout:` member arranges them, while one without positions them by their own `x`/`y`.

A child is also how anything that is not a view joins the tree: a `Dataset`, a `Spring`, a
`Keys` or `Focus` service, a stream. A source of events is a child, so it lives and dies with
the node that declares it; there is nothing to subscribe to and nothing to unregister.

child.gist: A child is a member that is itself an instance.

rules.rule: A child may not take an attribute's name — members share one namespace.
rules.says: App.width is an attribute — a child may not take an attribute's name

rules.rule: Two children cannot share a name.
rules.says: App.a: 'a' is already a child (first at line 1, col 7) — members share one namespace

rules.rule: A child cannot be named after a scope noun.
rules.says: 'this' is a scope noun (language §11) — a child cannot take its name

example.name: form-child
example.title: Named, anonymous, and non-visual children
example.lead: The named box is reached by name from a sibling; the anonymous texts are placed and painted; the Spring is a child too — it lives with the node that declares it. Click.
example.source:
App [ fill = 0xF6F8FA, textColor = 0x172530, fontSize = 14,
    open: boolean = false,
    onClick() { open = !open },
    box: View [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 60, height = 60, cornerRadius = 10, fill = 0x2E6FE0,
        Spring [ attribute = width, to = { app.open ? 260 : 60 }, stiffness = 160, damping = 20 ]
        ],
    Text [ x = 20, y = 92, text = { "the box is " + Math.round(app.box.width) + "px wide" } ],
    Text [ x = 20, y = 116, fontSize = 12, textColor = 0x6A7883, text = "later siblings paint on top; there is no z-index" ]
    ]

method.name: name(a: T) -> R { … }
syntax: name(v: number, c: Menu?) -> string { statements }
method.syntaxText:
name() { statements }
name(v: number, c: Menu?) -> string { statements }
method.lead:
A method is a typed signature, name first, and a statement body. Every parameter carries a
written type — a primitive, a component class, an event payload, a function type
(`f: (id: string) -> void`), or an array of one; a `?` after the type says the value may be
absent, and the body must check. Omit `-> R` for a method that returns nothing.

A method runs when called; an attribute stays true. A computed *value* is therefore not a
method but a declaration with a `{ }` default. A constraint that calls a method stays live
through it: every read inside the method is a wired dependency, rebased onto what you passed
— which is the difference between a method and a `script { }` function, whose body the
compiler never reads.

method.gist: A method is a typed signature, name first, and a statement body.

rules.rule: Parameters are typed; a bare name has no type.
rules.says: parameter 'a' has no type — a signature is typed name-first: 'f(a: number)'

rules.rule: Type annotations do not live in bodies: a local takes no annotation (contextual typing covers it); narrow with a cast (`x as T`), and put declared types on attributes.
rules.says: annotates a binding ('x') — bindings in a body take no type annotation (contextual typing covers them); a cast narrows an expression (x as T), and declared types live on the attribute (name: type = …)

rules.rule: A value slot takes one expression; statements live in methods.
rules.says: an attribute value is one expression, not statements; move the logic into a method and call it (e.g. { classroot.compute() })

example.name: form-method
example.title: A typed method, and a constraint that calls it
example.lead: `price()` is a method with typed parameters and a return type. The total is a constraint that calls it — and stays live through it, because the compiler reads the method's body.

handler.name: onEvent(e: Payload) { … }
handler.lead:
A handler is a method named `on` + an event this node fires — `onClick`, `onPointerMove`,
`onInit`, `onKeyDown` — and it is a method in every respect: a subclass's `onInit` replaces
its base's, and reaches it with `super.onInit()` when it wants the base's to run. The payload, when there is one, is typed by the event, and the
compiler names the type when you write the wrong one. Handlers only assign attributes; every
constraint that reads those attributes follows, which is the whole update model.

Nothing bubbles. A handler runs on the node that declares it, for events that node fires;
a parent that wants a child's click declares the handler on the child (or the child calls
up through `parent` or `classroot`). Events from outside the tree arrive as children — a
`Keys [ onKeyUp(e: KeyEvent) { … } ]` gives a node app-wide keyboard handling.
